summary: Washington says it wants a trade deal that accommodates Canada, Ottawa presses Stellantis over Brampton, and a plan to speed land purchases for high-speed rail draws fire.
body: US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on Wednesday that the US wants a deal that "accommodates" Canada on steel, aluminum and autos, which now face 25% US tariffs that President Trump has said will double to 50% on Jan. 1.[^1] Canadian Press reports the US offered to cut the auto tariff to 15%, but without an exemption for cars made under North American trade rules, and Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc says Canada is not about to sign.[^2] Canada was not among the 14 economies hit by new US tariff proposals this week (see World).

In Ontario, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly called a meeting with Stellantis "productive" after Ottawa served notice that the company broke a 2022 deal worth up to $529 million to retool its Brampton and Windsor plants.[^3] Stellantis moved Jeep production from Brampton to Illinois last year, laying off more than 2,000 workers, and has agreed to sell the plant to defence maker Roshel, which says it could create more than 2,000 jobs, with laid-off workers first in line.[^3]

Ottawa is also defending a plan, tucked into a 500-page budget motion, to give the Alto high-speed rail project wider powers to expropriate land, meaning to take it from owners with compensation. The roughly 1,000 km line from Toronto to Quebec City would cross 8,000 to 10,000 parcels and cost an estimated $60 billion to $90 billion.[^4] Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon says there is "no removal of due process"; the Conservatives and the Bloc call the change heavy-handed.[^4]

And Immigration Minister Lena Diab says a one-time plan to grant permanent residence will be capped at 200,000 people, half of them temporary workers chosen by provinces. Conservatives say it could strain housing; the government says most of those people already live here.[^5]
differences: On Alto, the government says landowners keep due process; Conservatives call it "a bulldozer" and the Bloc calls it authoritarian.[^4] On immigration, Conservatives warn of strain on housing and jobs, while Ottawa says most applicants are already in Canada.[^5]
